questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Identify the change that alters an antibiotic's binding site
questions.stem: Translator note TN-118 flags the phrase target changed and asks which kind of change actually alters the site the drug binds to.

options.text: A change in the membrane permeability of the organism, so less drug enters
options.misconception: confuses target alteration with reduced drug entry

options.text: An increase in the number of copies of the drug target inside the cell
options.misconception: believes more target copies equal a changed target

options.text: A mutation in the target protein that reduces the antibiotic's binding affinity
A deletion of the transporter that normally brings the antibiotic into the cell
options.misconception: mistakes loss of uptake for a modified target

questions.explanation: Altered targets arise when a mutation changes the protein the antibiotic binds, so the drug no longer inhibits it. Changing permeability or copy number alters drug concentration, not the binding site.
questions.hint: Think about the structure the drug attaches to.

options.text: The biofilm state makes cells far less permeable and less vulnerable to the drug

options.misconception: confuses a physiological state with a different species

questions.topic: Antibiotics: Reading a Zone of Inhibition
questions.learningObjective: Interpret why two discs of one drug give different zone sizes
questions.stem: Translator note TN-336 describes a plate where one disc has a clear zone of 28 mm and the neighbouring disc of the same drug has a clear zone of 8 mm; what does the smaller zone tell you?

options.text: That the second disc contained a weaker concentration of the antibiotic
options.misconception: blames the drug preparation for a smaller zone

options.text: That the second bacterial strain is completely resistant to the antibiotic
options.misconception: treats a smaller zone as complete resistance

options.text: That the second plate was incubated too long, giving any resistant cells time to grow
options.misconception: explains a small zone by incubation time alone

options.text: That the second inoculum is much heavier, so the drug is diluted in the agar near the disc

questions.explanation: Zone size depends on sensitivity, drug concentration and inoculum density, so a smaller zone with the same drug usually means a heavier inoculum. Complete resistance gives no zone at all.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Correct a reported minimum inhibitory concentration
questions.stem: Translator note TN-445 says the report described an MIC of 0.5 micrograms per millilitre although the lowest tube with no growth held 2 micrograms per millilitre.

options.text: MIC values are always reported as the lowest concentration that still allows growth
options.misconception: inverts the definition of the MIC endpoint

options.text: The value should have been the highest concentration showing no growth, which was 2 micrograms per millilitre
Values should be halved to convert them into a standard reporting convention
options.misconception: invents a halving rule that no protocol uses

options.text: The figure is correct because the report quoted the value in milligrams rather than micrograms
options.misconception: blames a unit convention the note never mentions

questions.explanation: The MIC is the lowest concentration that prevents visible growth, so it comes from the clear tubes, here 2 micrograms per millilitre. Quoting the last tube with growth gives the wrong number.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Describe how a resistance plasmid passes between bacteria
questions.stem: Translator note TN-554 asks for a plain-language account of how a resistance plasmid travels between bacteria in a crowded hospital sink.

answer.exemplar: Conjugation is the direct cell-to-cell transfer of DNA, usually through a conjugative plasmid. A donor bacterium forms a sex pilus, makes contact with a recipient and transfers a single-stranded copy of the plasmid, which the recipient resolves into a double-stranded circle. Because the plasmid carries its own origin of replication and often antibiotic resistance genes, the recipient becomes resistant and can pass the plasmid on in turn.

questions.explanation: Conjugation moves DNA by direct contact, so the plasmid is copied and resolved into a circle in the recipient, which becomes resistant and can donate again. It need not be a close relative.
questions.hint: Think about cell-to-cell contact.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the percentage of recipients that became transconjugants
questions.stem: In a conjugation experiment, 3.0×10^8 recipient cells were mixed with 1.0×10^8 donor cells carrying a resistance plasmid. After one hour, 4.5×10^5 recipients had received the plasmid. What percentage of the recipients were transconjugants?
questions.explanation: The proportion is 4.5×10^5 divided by 3.0×10^8, which is 1.5×10^-3, so 0.15 per cent of recipients received the plasmid. Using the total cell count as the denominator would understate the transfer frequency.
questions.hint: Divide transconjugants by the number of recipients.

options.misconception: claims replication speed blocks antibiotic action

options.misconception: doubles the numerator when computing the first rate

options.text: The prevalence fell by half in the number of patients, which counts as a 50 per cent fall
options.misconception: confuses counts with rates when the denominators differ

options.misconception: computes a percentage from two raw counts

options.text: The prevalence fell from 20 per cent to 10 per cent, a fall of 10 percentage points

questions.learningObjective: Interpret a plateau with slightly rising turbidity
questions.stem: Translator note TN-881 sketches a growth curve where the vertical axis rises a little further but the colony count stays level through the final stretch.

options.text: The cells are dead and the turbidity is caused by debris rather than living cells
options.misconception: reads an unchanged colony count as complete cell death

options.text: The cells are still growing larger while division and death are in balance
The culture is in the death phase, so cells are being lost faster than they are replaced
options.misconception: labels a flat count as active death phase

options.text: The measurement has saturated the spectrophotometer and can no longer detect change
options.misconception: blames instrument saturation for a flat count

questions.explanation: A plateau with rising turbidity is stationary phase, where nutrient limits make division balance death. Cells keep enlarging and stay active, so turbidity creeps up while the count holds.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Diagnose a failed plaque assay caused by blocked protein synthesis
questions.stem: Translator note TN-990 records that a phage sample produced no plaques after the bacteria were pre-treated with a drug that stops protein synthesis.

options.text: The drug also killed the bacterial lawn, so there was nothing left to infect
options.misconception: blames the lawn when the drug blocks phage replication

options.text: The phages were absorbed onto the plastic and never reached the bacteria
options.misconception: invokes tube adsorption with no supporting data

options.text: The drug blocked the phage's protein synthesis, so no new virus particles were made
Phage plaques require bacterial growth, so a static lawn always prevents them
options.misconception: overgeneralises a general rule to a drug-specific effect

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why each isolate must be susceptibility tested separately
questions.stem: Translator note TN-099 asks why a laboratory must test each isolate separately instead of assuming every strain of a species responds to the same drug.

answer.exemplar: Resistance by altered target arises from point mutations in the gene encoding the protein the antibiotic binds. Those mutations spread between related strains and even between species, and they accumulate where antibiotic use is heaviest. Because each isolate carries its own set of mutations, a result obtained for one strain cannot be transferred to another, and the laboratory must run susceptibility testing on each one.

questions.explanation: Altered targets come from mutations in the protein each antibiotic binds, and they accumulate where antibiotic pressure is high. Since mutation is chance, each isolate carries its own set and needs testing.
questions.hint: Remember that mutations arise independently.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate a biofilm count from a tolerance factor and a planktonic count
questions.stem: A biofilm on a catheter holds a viable count 1000 times higher than the planktonic cells exposed to the same antibiotic concentration. If the planktonic count is 2.0×10^3 CFU per mL, what is the biofilm count in CFU per mL?
questions.explanation: Multiplying the planktonic count by the tolerance factor gives 1000 times 2.0×10^3, which is 2.0×10^6 CFU per millilitre. Dividing instead of multiplying, or forgetting the factor of a thousand, are the usual errors here.
questions.hint: Apply the tolerance factor to the planktonic count.

options.text: The disc itself has a known inhibitory effect that must be subtracted from the measurement
options.misconception: credits the disc rather than the drug for the clear area

options.text: Measuring from the plate edge avoids having to measure the disc diameter at all
options.misconception: suggests plate-edge measurement removes the need for a control

Measuring from the disc edge gives a larger number, which makes the strain look more resistant

questions.learningObjective: Read the MIC endpoint from a dilution series
questions.stem: Translator note TN-217 shows a dilution series with growth at 0.5, 1 and 2 micrograms per millilitre and no growth at 4 and 8 micrograms per millilitre.

options.text: The minimum inhibitory concentration is 4 micrograms per millilitre, the lowest clear tube
The minimum inhibitory concentration is 0.5 micrograms per millilitre, the lowest tube tested
options.misconception: picks the lowest concentration rather than the lowest effective one

options.text: The minimum inhibitory concentration is 8 micrograms per millilitre, the highest tube tested
options.misconception: takes the top of the series as the endpoint

options.text: The minimum inhibitory concentration is 2 micrograms per millilitre, the last tube that grew
options.misconception: reads the endpoint from the last tube with growth

questions.learningObjective: Identify conjugation from a diagram of two joined cells
questions.stem: Translator note TN-326 draws two bacteria joined by a thin bridge with a plasmid loop shown inside the donor and a single strand entering the recipient.

options.text: Transformation, in which naked DNA released from dead cells is taken up from the medium
options.misconception: names the free DNA route for a direct contact diagram

options.text: Transduction, in which a bacteriophage carries bacterial DNA from one cell to another
options.misconception: confuses a phage carrier with direct cell contact

options.text: Vertical transmission, in which the plasmid is inherited by the daughter cells
options.misconception: treats ordinary cell division as gene transfer between cells

options.text: Conjugation, in which DNA is copied and transferred from a donor into a recipient cell

questions.explanation: A bridge between two cells with a strand moving from donor to recipient is conjugation, and the recipient can then pass the plasmid on. Transformation uses free DNA and transduction needs a phage.
questions.hint: Look for the physical connection between the cells.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Assess whether a shared plasmid proves direct transmission
questions.stem: Translator note TN-435 says a laboratory concluded that a resistant clone had spread between patients, but the only evidence was that two patients carried the same resistance plasmid.

options.text: Finding the same plasmid in two patients is conclusive proof of patient-to-patient spread
options.misconception: treats a shared plasmid as conclusive transmission evidence

options.text: Plasmid identity alone does not prove direct transfer, since plasmids can persist and spread independently
The conclusion is sound because resistant bacteria always transfer plasmids directly between hosts
options.misconception: assumes host-to-host transfer is the only route

options.text: The plasmid must have moved by conjugation because conjugation is the only way DNA moves
options.misconception: assumes conjugation is the only horizontal transfer route

questions.explanation: A plasmid can spread by many routes, including a shared antibiotic source or contaminated food, so sharing one does not prove direct host-to-host transmission. Epidemiological links are needed too.
questions.hint: Ask what else could carry the same plasmid.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Compare the drug targets available in bacteria and viruses
questions.stem: Translator note TN-544 asks for a short passage explaining why the same antibiotic fails against a viral infection yet works against a bacterial one.

answer.exemplar: Antibiotics act on structures that exist only in bacteria, chiefly the peptidoglycan cell wall and the 70S ribosomal subunit. A virus has neither: it is a particle of nucleic acid in a protein coat that must enter a living host cell and use that cell's ribosomes and enzymes to copy itself. Because there is no bacterial target, antibiotics cannot act, and an antiviral agent is required instead.

questions.explanation: Antibiotics act on bacterial structures such as peptidoglycan and the 70S ribosome, and a virus has neither, so no target exists. Viruses hide inside host cells and borrow their machinery.
questions.hint: Compare the target structures in both organisms.

The culture is in the log phase, since the count would otherwise have risen steadily

options.text: The culture is in the death phase, since cells are being lost faster than they are replaced
options.misconception: labels a stationary culture as declining

options.text: The culture has died out completely, because no further colonies can be detected
options.misconception: reads an unchanged count as total death

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish lysogeny from a lytic infection using culture evidence
questions.stem: Translator note TN-762 reports that a bacterial strain exposed to a temperate phage showed no lysis but later produced phage when a stress agent was applied.

options.text: The phage had completed a lytic cycle, so new virions were already waiting to infect
options.misconception: claims a lytic cycle while no lysis was observed

options.text: The bacteria had become resistant to the phage, so the stress had no effect on them
options.misconception: invokes phage resistance without any supporting evidence

questions.learningObjective: Explain treatment failure caused by a device-associated biofilm

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Antibiotics: Reading a Zone of Inhibition
questions.learningObjective: Explain why identical discs can produce different zone sizes
questions.stem: Translator note TN-109 asks for a paragraph explaining why two identical antibiotic discs can give different zone sizes on the same plate.

answer.exemplar: Two discs of the same drug and strength can still differ if the lawns they sit on differ. A heavier inoculum contains more cells per millilitre, and each cell has to be inhibited independently, so the drug is used up more quickly and the clear zone shrinks. Spacing the discs too close lets one zone overlap the other and distort the gradient, so standard methods keep a fixed distance between discs.

questions.explanation: Zone size depends on inoculum density, diffusion rate and sensitivity, so identical discs can differ if the lawn or spacing differs. Comparing zones without checking those variables is the trap.
questions.hint: List the variables that change a zone.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why batch cultures are harvested during the log phase
questions.stem: Translator note TN-656 asks for an explanation of why a batch culture must be harvested during the log phase if the aim is a high yield of biomass.

answer.exemplar: In the log phase cells divide at a constant rate and the population rises exponentially, so biomass increases fastest and the yield per unit substrate is high. In the stationary phase growth has stopped because nutrients are exhausted and waste has accumulated, so further incubation adds no cells and may even reduce yield as cells lyse and the substrate is wasted on maintenance.

questions.explanation: Log phase is where exponential growth occurs, so biomass accumulates fastest, whereas stationary phase adds no cells because nutrients are exhausted. Waiting too long wastes substrate on maintenance.
questions.hint: Think about when the population is multiplying fastest.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why resistance to one drug in a class does not imply resistance to all
questions.stem: Translator note TN-765 asks why an isolate resistant to one beta-lactam may still be sensitive to a related one.

options.text: The mutation altered the whole cell so that every antibiotic in the class is blocked
options.misconception: assumes one mutation blocks an entire drug class

options.text: The isolate is sensitive only because the plate was left out too long
options.misconception: invokes a plate timing error with no evidence

Resistance to one drug always signals resistance to every related drug

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Describe the mechanics of plasmid transfer between species
questions.stem: Translator note TN-195 asks for a description of how a plasmid carrying antibiotic resistance can pass from one bacterial species to another inside a human gut.

answer.exemplar: A conjugative plasmid carries the tra genes needed to build a sex pilus and a type IV secretion apparatus. When a donor cell makes contact with a recipient of another species, one strand of the plasmid is transferred through the conjugation channel and is converted into a double-stranded circle in the recipient. The recipient is now resistant and, having the tra genes itself, can pass the plasmid to further cells, so the element spreads through the community.

questions.explanation: Conjugation needs the donor to supply the DNA and the transfer machinery, and works across species, so a plasmid can move between unrelated bacteria. The recipient becomes a donor in turn.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Contrast altered target resistance with increased target production
questions.stem: Translator note TN-626 asks for a comparison of altered target resistance with increased target production.

answer.exemplar: Altered target resistance works by changing the shape of the protein so that the drug fits less well, which usually needs only one or a few point mutations and does not slow bacterial growth. Resistance by increased target production works differently: the cell makes many more copies of the target, so a drug concentration that once blocked growth is no longer enough, and this often carries a fitness cost because extra target protein is wasteful.

questions.explanation: Altered target resistance changes the binding site itself by point mutation, whereas increased target production raises the amount of protein. The first is often costless, the second usually slows growth.
questions.hint: Ask whether the protein itself changed.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain the differing responses of bacteria and viruses to one antimicrobial
questions.stem: Translator note TN-175 asks for an explanation of why bacteria and viruses respond so differently to the same antimicrobial treatment.

answer.exemplar: Bacteria are free-living cells with their own peptidoglycan wall, their own 70S ribosomes and their own DNA replication machinery, so antibiotics have specific handles to grip. Viruses have none of these: they are nucleic acid in a protein coat that can only multiply by borrowing the ribosomes and enzymes of a host cell. A drug aimed at a bacterial handle therefore has nothing to hold in a virus, and it can even leave the host cell unharmed while the virus continues to copy.

questions.explanation: Antibiotics exploit handles only bacteria have, such as peptidoglycan and the 70S ribosome, while viruses borrow host machinery. One compound can block a bacterium completely and leave a virus replicating.
questions.hint: Compare what each organism has to offer a drug.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Antibiotics: Reading a Zone of Inhibition
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a larger zone indicates a more effective antibiotic
questions.stem: Translator note TN-624 asks for a passage explaining why a larger zone of inhibition is taken to mean a more effective antibiotic.

answer.exemplar: Antibiotic released from a disc spreads through the agar and forms a concentration gradient that is highest at the disc and falls steadily outwards. Growth is stopped wherever the concentration exceeds the level needed to inhibit the organism, so the width of the clear zone measures how far that inhibitory level reached. A larger zone therefore means the drug inhibits at lower concentrations, which is the practical measure of how useful it will be.

questions.explanation: The clear zone marks the distance over which drug concentration stayed above the inhibitory threshold, so a wider zone means inhibition at lower concentration. Zone width compares potency in practice.
questions.hint: Think about the concentration gradient in the agar.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why continuous culture outperforms batch culture for yield
questions.stem: Translator note TN-277 asks for a paragraph on why a continuous culture is often preferred to a batch culture for making large amounts of bacterial product.

answer.exemplar: In a batch culture the organism grows until nutrients run out and then sits in stationary phase, so most of the vessel is filled with resting cells rather than producing ones. A continuous culture keeps dilute fresh medium flowing in and wastes out, so cells remain in the log phase and keep dividing at a constant rate. That converts a large part of the vessel into active production and makes the output predictable and easy to control.

questions.explanation: A batch culture stops growing once nutrients run out, whereas a continuous culture holds cells in the log phase and keeps production steady, giving better yield per volume over long runs.
